extraction_notes.note: Section 5 restates verbatim the definitions of section 4 (a, q, psi_a as numbered equation (5.1), Poisson kernel and Psi_kappa as numbered equation (5.10)). Treated as restated copies: no nodes for (5.1)/(5.10), and the one \ref to (5.10) (proof of Lemma 5.3) is covered by a hand edge from the section-4 definition.

Simple manifolds are defined twice (Definition 1.3 and again in prose in Section 2.1 via convex non-trapping + no conjugate points); the prose copy and the Section 1.2 copy of K^+, k^+ (restated with numbers (2.8)-(2.9) in Section 2.2) got no node.
remark or claim+proof: the construction of solutions to the two transport equations is a derivation in running text with no separately stated result, so each is kept as one remark.

numbered equations named in the text (Gauss-Ostrogradskii formulas, Pestov identity, divergence formula, Green's formula) were retyped as external theorems; the unnamed commutation formulas (2.24)-(2.25) stayed equations.

Theorem 1.4 and Theorem 2.1 have no proof environment; their proofs are split across sections (end of 4.2 and end of 5; density remark in 2.2 and the starred subsection), extracted as one prose proof per part.

Literature results summarized in Section 1.3 (Rakesh-Symes, Isakov, Sun, Stefanov-Uhlmann, Montalto, Belishev-Kurylev, ...) are described loosely and related to nothing in the argument; only the gauge-invariance statement was extracted. Physical motivation and the Einstein summation convention were also left out.

Several typos in the source (Lemma 4.1 cites transport equation (3.7) instead of (3.11); Lambda_{q_2,q_2} in (4.9); Lemma 3.3 has no proof beyond 'By similar way'); statements copied verbatim, and Lemma 3.3 marked semi_formal.

nodes.statement: Let $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ be an $n$-dimensional ($n\geq 2$) compact Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary $\partial\mathrm{M}$ where $\mathrm{g}$ denotes a Riemannian metric of class $\mathcal{C}^\infty$.

nodes.statement: We let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace-Beltrami operator on $\mathrm{M}$.

nodes.statement: Given $T>0$, we denote $Q=\mathrm{M}\times(0,T)$ and $\Sigma=\partial\mathrm{M}\times(0,T)$.

nodes.name: Derivation of the uniqueness corollary
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{Th2}, we can readily derive the following uniqueness result
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the Hölder stability estimate of Theorem 1.4.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of absorption coefficient and potential
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ be a simple compact Riemannian manifold with boundary of dimension $n \geq 2$, such that $k^+(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})<1$ and let $T>\textrm{Diam}_\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{M})$, we have that $\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}=\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}$ implies $a_1 =a_2$ and $q_1=q_2$ almost everywhere in $\mathrm{M}$.
nodes.statement_short: Equal DN maps force $a_1=a_2$ and $q_1=q_2$ a.e.
assumptions: Let $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ be a simple compact Riemannian manifold with boundary of dimension $n \geq 2$, such that $k^+(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})<1$ and let $T>\textrm{Diam}_\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{M})$

nodes.name: Gauge invariance of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map
nodes.statement: As was noted in \cite{[SU]}, the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map is invariant under a gauge transformation of the metric~$\mathrm{g}$. Namely, given a diffeomorphism $\psi:\mathrm{M}\to \mathrm{M}$ such that $\psi|_{\partial\mathrm{M}}={\rm Id}$ one has $\Lambda_{\psi^*\mathrm{g},a,\,q}=\Lambda_{\mathrm{g},a,\,q}$ where $\psi^*\mathrm{g}$ denotes the pullback of the metric $\mathrm{g}$ under $\psi$.
assumptions: given a diffeomorphism $\psi:\mathrm{M}\to \mathrm{M}$ such that $\psi|_{\partial\mathrm{M}}={\rm Id}$

nodes.name: Inverse problem for absorption coefficient and electric potential
nodes.statement: In this paper, the inverse problem under consideration is whether, for a fixed metric $\mathrm{g}$, the knowledge of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_{\mathrm{g},a,\,q}$ on the boundary uniquely determines the electric potential $q$ and the absorption coefficient $a$.
nodes.statement_short: Does the DN map for a fixed metric determine both $q$ and $a$?

nodes.name: Geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}$
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ be a Riemannian manifold, for $x\in \mathrm{M}$ and $\xi\in T_x\mathrm{M}$ we let $\gamma_{x,\xi}$ denote the unique geodesic starting at the point $x$ in the direction $\xi$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Sphere bundle and co-sphere bundle
nodes.statement: By \begin{align*} S\mathrm{M}=\set{(x,\xi)\in T\mathrm{M};\,\abs{\xi}=1}, \quad S^*\mathrm{M}=\set{(x,p)\in T^*\mathrm{M};\,\abs{p}=1}, \end{align*} we denote the sphere bundle and co-sphere bundle of $\mathrm{M}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Exponential map
nodes.statement: The exponential map $\exp_x:T_x\mathrm{M}\to \mathrm{M}$ is given by \begin{equation} \exp_x(v)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(\abs{v}),\quad \xi=\frac{v\,\,}{\abs{v}}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Equation (2.1)
nodes.statement: \exp_x(v)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(\abs{v}),\quad \xi=\frac{v\,\,}{\abs{v}}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Convex non-trapping manifold
nodes.statement: A compact Riemannian manifold $(\mathrm{M},\, \mathrm{g})$ with boundary is called a convex non-trapping manifold, if it satisfies two conditions: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] the boundary $\partial \mathrm{M}$ is strictly convex, i.e., the second fundamental form of the boundary is positive definite at every boundary point, \item[(ii)] all geodesics having finite length in $\mathrm{M}$, i.e., for each $(x,\xi) \in S\mathrm{M}$, the maximal geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)$ satisfying the initial conditions $\gamma_{x,\xi}(0) = x$ and $\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(0) = \xi$ is defined on a finite segment with extremities $\ell_{-}(x,\xi)$ and $\ell_{+}(x,\xi)$. We recall that a geodesic $\gamma: [a, b] \longrightarrow M$ is maximal if it cannot be extended to a segment $[a-\varepsilon_1, b+\varepsilon_2]$, where $\varepsilon_i \geq 0$ and $\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 > 0$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold
differentia: all geodesics having finite length in $\mathrm{M}$
nodes.statement_short: Strictly convex boundary and every maximal geodesic has finite length.

nodes.name: Topology of simple manifolds
nodes.statement: A simple $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold is diffeomorphic to a closed ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and any pair of points in the manifold are joined by an unique geodesic.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold
conclusions: is diffeomorphic to a closed ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$
any pair of points in the manifold are joined by an unique geodesic

nodes.name: Exit times $\ell_\pm$
nodes.statement: Let $(x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M}$, there exist a unique geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}$ associated to $(x,\xi)$ which is maxmimally defined on a finite intervall $[\ell_-(x,\xi),\ell_+(x,\xi)]$, with $\gamma_{x,\xi}(\ell_\pm(x,\xi))\in\partial\mathrm{M}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Geodesic flow
nodes.statement: We define the geodesic flow $\phi_t$ as following \begin{equation} \phi_t:S\mathrm{M}\to S\mathrm{M},\quad \phi_t(x,\xi)=(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(t)),\quad t\in [\ell_-(x,\xi),\ell_+(x,\xi)], \end{equation} and $\phi_t$ is a flow, that is, $\phi_t\circ\phi_s=\phi_{t+s}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Equation (2.2)
nodes.statement: \phi_t:S\mathrm{M}\to S\mathrm{M},\quad \phi_t(x,\xi)=(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(t)),\quad t\in [\ell_-(x,\xi),\ell_+(x,\xi)],
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Inner and outer boundary vectors $\partial_\pm S\mathrm{M}$
nodes.statement: Now, we introduce the submanifolds of inner and outer vectors of $S\mathrm{M}$ \begin{equation} \partial_{\pm}S\mathrm{M} =\set{(x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M},\, x \in \partial \mathrm{M},\, \pm\seq{\xi,\nu(x)}< 0}, \end{equation} where $\nu$ is the unit outer normal to the boundary.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Equation (2.3)
nodes.statement: \partial_{\pm}S\mathrm{M} =\set{(x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M},\, x \in \partial \mathrm{M},\, \pm\seq{\xi,\nu(x)}< 0},
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Properties of the exit-time functions $\ell_\pm$
nodes.statement: Thus we can define two functions $\ell_\pm:S\mathrm{M}\to\mathbb{R}$ which satisfy $$ \ell_-(x,\xi)\leq 0,\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)\geq 0,\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)=-\ell_-(x,-\xi), $$ $$ \ell_-(x,\xi)=0,\quad (x,\xi)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M},\quad \ell_+(x,\xi)=0,\quad (x,\xi)\in\partial_-S\mathrm{M}, $$ $$ \ell_-(\phi_t(x,\xi))=\ell_-(x,\xi)-t,\quad \ell_+(\phi_t(x,\xi))=\ell_+(x,\xi)-t. $$
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold
nodes.statement_short: $\ell_-\le0\le\ell_+$, they vanish on $\partial_\pm S\mathrm{M}$ respectively and decrease by $t$ along the flow.

nodes.name: Smoothness of $\ell_\pm$
nodes.statement: Concerning smoothness properties of $\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$, we can see that these functions are smooth near a point $(x,\xi)$ such that the geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)$ intersects $\partial\mathrm{M}$ transversely for $t=\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$. By strict convexity of $\partial\mathrm{M}$, the functions $\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$ are smooth on $T\mathrm{M} \setminus T(\partial\mathrm{M}).$ In fact, all points of $T\mathrm{M} \cap T(\partial\mathrm{M})$ are singular for $\ell_{\pm}$; since some derivatives of these functions are unbounded in a neighbourhood of such points. In particular, $\ell_{+}$ is smooth on $\partial_+SM$, see Lemma 4.1.1 of \cite{[Sh]}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold
conclusions: the functions $\ell_{\pm}(x,\xi)$ are smooth on $T\mathrm{M} \setminus T(\partial\mathrm{M}).$
nodes.statement_short: $\ell_\pm$ are smooth away from $T(\partial M)$, singular on it; $\ell_+$ is smooth on $\partial_+SM$.

nodes.name: Volume form on $S_x\mathrm{M}$
nodes.statement: The Riemannian scalar product on $T_x\mathrm{M}$ induces the volume form on $S_x\mathrm{M}$, denoted by $\mathrm{d} \omega_x(\xi)$ and given by $$ \mathrm{d} \omega_x(\xi)=\sqrt{\abs{\mathrm{g}}} \, \sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^k\xi^k \mathrm{d} \xi^1\wedge\cdots\wedge \widehat{\mathrm{d} \xi^k}\wedge\cdots\wedge \mathrm{d} \xi^n. $$
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Liouville volume form on $S\mathrm{M}$
nodes.statement: We introduce the volume form $\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}$ on the manifold $S\mathrm{M}$ by $$ \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} (x,\xi)=\mathrm{d}\omega_x(\xi)\wedge \,\mathrm{dv}^{n}, $$ where $\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}$ is the Riemannnian volume form on $\mathrm{M}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Liouville's theorem
nodes.statement: By Liouville's theorem, the form $\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}$ is preserved by the geodesic flow.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold
conclusions: the form $\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}$ is preserved by the geodesic flow

nodes.name: Volume form on $\partial S\mathrm{M}$
nodes.statement: The corresponding volume form on the boundary $\partial S\mathrm{M} =\set{(x,\xi)\in S\mathrm{M},\, x\in\partial \mathrm{M}}$ is given by $$ \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}=\mathrm{d}\omega_x(\xi) \wedge \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1}, $$ where $\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1}$ is the volume form of $\partial \mathrm{M}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Weighted space $L^2_\mu(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})$
nodes.statement: Let $L^2_\mu(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})$ be the space of square integrable functions with respect to the measure $\mu(x,\xi)\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}$ with $\mu(x,\xi)=\abs{\seq{\xi,\nu(x)}}$. This Hilbert space is endowed with the scalar product \begin{equation} \para{u,v}_\mu=\int_{\partial_+S\mathrm{M}}u(x,\xi) \overline{v}(x,\xi) \mu(x,\xi)\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Equation (2.4)
nodes.statement: \para{u,v}_\mu=\int_{\partial_+S\mathrm{M}}u(x,\xi) \overline{v}(x,\xi) \mu(x,\xi)\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Geodesic X-ray transform
nodes.statement: The ray transform (also called geodesic $X$-ray transform) on a convex non trapping manifold $\mathrm{M}$ is the linear operator \begin{equation} \mathcal{I}:\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathrm{M})\longrightarrow \mathcal{C}^\infty(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}), \end{equation} defined by the equality \begin{equation} \mathcal{I} f(x,\xi)=\int_0^{\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t))\, \mathrm{d} t,\quad (x,\xi)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{I}f(x,\xi)$ integrates $f$ along the geodesic from $(x,\xi)\in\partial_+SM$ to its exit time.

nodes.name: Equation (2.5)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{I}:\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathrm{M})\longrightarrow \mathcal{C}^\infty(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}),
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Equation (2.6)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{I} f(x,\xi)=\int_0^{\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t))\, \mathrm{d} t,\quad (x,\xi)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Boundedness of the ray transform on Sobolev spaces
nodes.statement: The ray transform on a convex non trapping manifold $\mathrm{M}$ can be extended as a bounded operator \begin{equation} \mathcal{I}:H^k(\mathrm{M})\longrightarrow H^k(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}), \end{equation} for every integer $k\geq 1$, see Theorem 4.2.1 of \cite{[Sh]}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold
assumptions: on a convex non trapping manifold $\mathrm{M}$
conclusions: can be extended as a bounded operator

nodes.name: Equation (2.7)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{I}:H^k(\mathrm{M})\longrightarrow H^k(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}),
nodes.section: 2.1 Geodesical ray transform on a simple manifold

nodes.name: Curvature tensor
nodes.statement:
Let $R$ be the curvature tensor of the Levi-Civita connection $
abla_X$ defined by $$ R(X,Y)Z=
abla_X
abla_Y Z+
abla_Y
abla_X Z-
abla_{[X,Y]} Z, \quad X,Y,Z\in T\mathrm{M}. $$
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Sectional curvature
nodes.statement: For a point $x \in \mathrm{M}$ and a two-dimensional subspace $\pi \subset T_x\mathrm{M},$ the number $$ K(x,\pi)=\frac{\langle R(\xi,\eta)\eta,\xi\rangle}{\vert \xi \vert^2 \vert \eta \vert^2-\langle \xi, \eta \rangle^2}, $$ is independent of the choice of the basis $\xi$, $\eta$ for $\pi$. It is called the sectional curvature of the manifold $\mathrm{M}$ at the point $x$ and in the two-dimentional direction $\pi$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Maximal positive sectional curvature $K^+(x,\xi)$
nodes.statement: For $(x,\xi)\in T\mathrm{M}$, we set $K(x,\xi)=\underset{\pi \ni \xi}{\sup} K(x,\pi) $ and \begin{equation} K^+(x,\xi)=\max\{0,K(x,\xi)\}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Equation (2.8)
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Curvature characteristic $k^+(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$
nodes.statement: For a simple compact Riemannian manifold $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$, we set \begin{equation} k^+(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})=\sup\lbrace \int_0^{\ell_+(x,\xi)} tK^+(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(t)) dt, \; (x,\xi)\in \partial_+S\mathrm{M}\rbrace. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform
nodes.statement_short: Supremum over boundary-starting geodesics of $\int t K^+(\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))dt$.

nodes.name: Equation (2.9)
nodes.statement: k^+(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})=\sup\lbrace \int_0^{\ell_+(x,\xi)} tK^+(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(t)) dt, \; (x,\xi)\in \partial_+S\mathrm{M}\rbrace.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Stability estimate for the geodesic X-ray transform
nodes.statement: For every simple compact Riemannian manifold $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ with $k^+(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})<1$, there exist $C>0$ such that the following stability estimate \begin{equation} \Vert f \Vert _{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}, \end{equation} holds for any $f\in H^1(\mathrm{M})$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform
nodes.statement_short: If $k^+(M,g)<1$, then $\|f\|_{L^2}\le C\|\mathcal{I}f\|_{H^1(\partial_+SM)}$.
assumptions: For every simple compact Riemannian manifold $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ with $k^+(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})<1$
conclusions: there exist $C>0$ such that the following stability estimate
nodes.label: theorem

nodes.name: Equation (2.10)
nodes.statement: \Vert f \Vert _{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})},
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1 (reduction to smooth functions)
nodes.statement: By density arguments, it suffices to prove the theorem for $f \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathrm{M})$. Indeed, if $f\in H^1(M)$, then we can find a sequence $(f_k)_k$ in $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathrm{M})$ converging towards $f$ in $H^1(\mathrm{M}).$ The ray transform $\mathcal{I}$ is a bounded operator from $H^1(\mathrm{M})$ into $H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})$, so the sequence $(\mathcal{I} f_k)_k$ converges towards $\mathcal{I} f$ in $H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}).$ Applying the theorem for $f_k$ and passing to the limit as $k \rightarrow +\infty,$ we deduce that $ \Vert f \Vert _{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform
nodes.statement_short: Density argument: reduce to smooth $f$ and pass to the limit using boundedness of $\mathcal{I}$ on $H^1$.

nodes.name: Reduction to smooth $f$
nodes.statement: By density arguments, it suffices to prove the theorem for $f \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathrm{M})$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to treat smooth $f$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Approximating sequence
nodes.statement: Indeed, if $f\in H^1(M)$, then we can find a sequence $(f_k)_k$ in $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathrm{M})$ converging towards $f$ in $H^1(\mathrm{M}).$
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $f$ by smooth $f_k$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Continuity of $\mathcal{I}$
nodes.statement: The ray transform $\mathcal{I}$ is a bounded operator from $H^1(\mathrm{M})$ into $H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})$, so the sequence $(\mathcal{I} f_k)_k$ converges towards $\mathcal{I} f$ in $H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}).$
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness of $\mathcal{I}$ gives convergence of $\mathcal{I}f_k$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: Applying the theorem for $f_k$ and passing to the limit as $k \rightarrow +\infty,$ we deduce that $ \Vert f \Vert _{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the limit in the estimate.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Bundle of tensors of degree $(r,s)$
nodes.statement: Let $\tau_s^r\mathrm{M}$ be the bundle of tensors of degree $(r,s)$ on $\mathrm{M}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Tensor field
nodes.statement: Its sections denoted by $T_s^r$ are called \textit{tensor fields of degree $(r,s)$.}
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Module of smooth tensor fields
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_s^r\mathrm{M},U)$ the $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(U)$-module of smooth sections of the bundle $\tau_s^r \mathrm{M}$ over $U$. The notation $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_s^r\mathrm{M},\mathrm{M})$ will usually be abbreviated to $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_s^r\mathrm{M}).$
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Coordinates of a tensor field
nodes.statement: If $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ is a local coordinate system defined in a domain $U$, then any tensor field $u\in \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_s^r \mathrm{M},U)$ can be uniquely represented as \begin{equation} u=u_{j_1,\dots,j_s}^{i_1,\dots,i_r} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_r}}\otimes dx^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes dx^{j_s}, \end{equation} where $u_{j_1,\cdots,j_s}^{i_1,\cdots,i_r} \in \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(U)$ are called the coordinates of the field $u$ in the given coordinate system.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Equation (2.11)
nodes.statement: u=u_{j_1,\dots,j_s}^{i_1,\dots,i_r} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_r}}\otimes dx^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes dx^{j_s},
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Equation (2.12)
nodes.statement: u=(u_{j_1,\cdots,j_s}^{i_1,\cdots,i_r}).
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Covariant derivative of a vector field
nodes.statement:
The bundles $	au_s^r \mathrm{M}$ and $	au_r^s \mathrm{M}$ are dual to each other and, consequently, $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(	au_s^r \mathrm{M})$ and $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(	au_r^s \mathrm{M})$ are mutually dual $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathrm{M})$-modules. This implies in particular that a field $u\in \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(	au_s^1 \mathrm{M})$ can be considered as a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathrm{M})$-multilinear mapping $u:\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(	au_0^1 \mathrm{M})	imes\dots	imes\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(	au_0^1 \mathrm{M})\longrightarrow \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(	au_0^1 \mathrm{M}).$ Consequently, a given connection $
abla$ on $\mathrm{M}$ defines the $\mathbb{C}$-linear mapping (denoted by the same letter)  egin{equation} 
abla:\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(	au_0^1 \mathrm{M})\longrightarrow \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(	au_1^1 \mathrm{M}) \end{equation} by the formula $(
abla v)(u)=
abla_uv,$ The tensor field $
abla v$ is called the 	extit{covariant derivative} of the vector field $v$ (with respect to the given connection).
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Equation (2.13)
nodes.statement: \nabla:\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_0^1 \mathrm{M})\longrightarrow \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_1^1 \mathrm{M})
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Covariant differentiation of tensor fields
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform
conclusions: The covariant differenciation defined on vector fields can be transferred to tensor fields
nodes.statement_short: Covariant differentiation extends from vector fields to all tensor fields, with the Christoffel-symbol coordinate formula.

nodes.name: Equation (2.14)
nodes.statement: \nabla:\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_s^r \mathrm{M})\longrightarrow \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_{s+1}^r \mathrm{M})
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Equation (2.15)
nodes.statement: \nabla_ku_{j_1\dots j_s}^{i_1\dots i_r} =\frac{\partial}{\partial x^k}u_{j_1\dots j_s}^{i_1 \dots i_r}+\sum_{m=1}^r\Gamma^{i_m}_{kp}u_{j_1 \dots j_s}^{i_1 \dots i_{m-1} p i_{m+1} \dots i_r}-\sum_{m=1}^s\Gamma^{p}_{kj_m}u_{j_1 \dots j_{m-1} p j_{m+1} \dots j_s}^{i_1 \dots i_r},
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Associated coordinate system on $T\mathrm{M}$
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be the projection on $\mathrm{M}$. On the domain $p^{-1}(U)\subset T\mathrm{M}$, the family of the functions $(x^1, \dots,x^n,\xi^1,\dots,\xi^n)$ is a local coordinate system which is called \textit{associated} with the system $(x^1,\dots,x^n).$
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Natural coordinate system
nodes.statement: A local coordinate system on $T\mathrm{M}$ will be called a \textit{natural coordinate system} if it is associated with some local coordinate system on $\mathrm{M}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Semibasic tensor
nodes.statement: A tensor $u \in T^r_{s,(x,\xi)}(T\mathrm{M})$ of degree $(r,s)$ at a point $(x,\xi)\in T\mathrm{M}$ is called \textit{semibasic} if in some (and so, in any) natural coordinate system, it can be represented as: \begin{equation} u=u_{j_1 \dots j_s}^{i_1 \dots i_r} \frac{\partial}{\partial \xi^{i_1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\frac{\partial}{\partial \xi^{i_r}}\otimes dx^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes dx^{j_s}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Equation (2.16)
nodes.statement: u=u_{j_1 \dots j_s}^{i_1 \dots i_r} \frac{\partial}{\partial \xi^{i_1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\frac{\partial}{\partial \xi^{i_r}}\otimes dx^{j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes dx^{j_s}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Bundle of semibasic tensors $\beta_s^r\mathrm{M}$
nodes.statement: We denote by $\beta_s^r\mathrm{M}$ the subbundle in $\tau_s^r(T\mathrm{M})$ made of all semibasic tensors of degree $(r,s).$
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Semibasic vector and covector fields
nodes.statement: The elements of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\beta_0^1 \mathrm{M})$ are called the \textit{semibasic vector fields}, and the elements of $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\beta_1^0 \mathrm{M})$ are called \textit{semibasic covector fields}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Canonical imbedding of tensor fields into semibasic fields
nodes.statement: Tensor fields on $M$ can be identified with the semibasic tensor fields on $T\mathrm{M}$ whose components are independent of the second argument $\xi$. Thus we obtain the canonical imbedding \begin{equation} \iota:\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\tau_s^r \mathrm{M}) \subset \mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\beta_s^r \mathrm{M}). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Properties of $u$: homogeneity and kinetic equation
nodes.statement: The function $u$ given by (\ref{2.34}) is smooth on $T\mathrm{M}\backslash T(\partial\mathrm{M})$ and has the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item $u$ is homogeneous function of degree $-1$ in $\xi$. \item $u$ satisfies the following kinetic equation $Hu=-f$. \item $u$ satisfies the following equation $H\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u=-\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement_short: $u$ is smooth off $T(\partial M)$, homogeneous of degree $-1$, solves $Hu=-f$ and $H\overset{v}{\nabla}u=-\overset{h}{\nabla}u$.
conclusions: $u$ is homogeneous function of degree $-1$ in $\xi$.
$u$ satisfies the following equation $H\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u=-\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform
nodes.statement_short: Item-by-item: scaling of $\ell_+$ and geodesics; differentiate along the flow; apply $\overset{v}{\nabla}$ and the commutation formulas.

nodes.name: Item (1): homogeneity
nodes.statement: Item (1) is immediate from the relations $\ell_+(x,\lambda \xi)=\frac{1}{\lambda}\ell_+(x,\xi)$ and $\gamma_{x,\lambda \xi}(t)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(\lambda t)$ for any $\lambda>0$. Then $$ u(x,\lambda \xi)=\int_0^{\frac{1}{\lambda}\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(\lambda t)) dt = \frac{1}{\lambda} u(x,\xi). $$
nodes.statement_short: Scaling of $\ell_+$ and geodesics gives homogeneity of degree $-1$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Item (2): kinetic equation
nodes.statement: Prove item (2). For $s \in \mathbb{R}$ sufficiently small, we set $x_s=\gamma_{x,\xi}(s)$ and $\xi_s=\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(s).$ Then, $\gamma_{x_s,\xi_s}(t)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(t+s)$ and $\ell_+(x_s,\xi_s)=\tau_+(x,\xi)-s.$ So, $$ u(\gamma_{x,\xi}(s),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(s))=u(x_s,\xi_s) = \int_0^{\ell_+(x_s,\xi_s)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t+s)) dt =\int_s^{\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)) dt . $$ Differentiating with respect to $s$ and taking $s=0$, we obtain that $$ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x_i}\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}^i(0)+\frac{\partial u}{\partial \xi_i} \ddot {\gamma}_{x,\xi}^{i}(0)=-f(x). $$ Since we have $\gamma_{x,\xi}(0)=x$, $\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(0)=\xi$ and $\ddot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}^{i}(0)=-\Gamma ^i_{jk}(x)\xi^j\xi^k,$ then $$\xi^i\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_i}-\Gamma^i_{jk}\xi^j\xi^k\frac{\partial u}{\partial \xi_i}= -f(x).$$ Thus we have $Hu=-f$.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate $u$ along the geodesic flow to get $Hu=-f$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Item (3): commuted equation
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\overset{v}{\nabla}$ to $Hu=-f$ and use the commutation relations.
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform

nodes.name: Curvature inequality for semibasic fields
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ be a simple Riemannian manifold and $K^+$ given by (\ref{2.8}). Let a semibasic tensor field $u\in\mathcal{C}^\infty(\beta_m^0\mathrm{M})$ satisfies boundary condition (\ref{2.36}), then the following inequality \begin{equation} \int_{S\mathrm{M}} K^+(x,\xi) \vert u(x,\xi) \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \leq k^+\int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert Hu(x,\xi) \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}. \end{equation} holds true. Here $k^+=k^+(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ is given by (\ref{2.9}).
nodes.section: 2.2 Inverse inequality for the geodesical ray-transform
nodes.statement_short: $\int K^+|u|^2\le k^+\int|Hu|^2$ over $SM$ for semibasic $u$ vanishing on $\partial_-SM$.
assumptions: Let $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ be a simple Riemannian manifold and $K^+$ given by (\ref{2.8}).
Let a semibasic tensor field $u\in\mathcal{C}^\infty(\beta_m^0\mathrm{M})$ satisfies boundary condition (\ref{2.36})

nodes.name: Equation (2.37)
nodes.statement: \int_{S\mathrm{M}} K^+(x,\xi) \vert u(x,\xi) \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \leq k^+\int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert Hu(x,\xi) \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1 (Pestov identity argument)
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the Pestov identity for $u$ over $SM$ and bound the curvature term by $k^+<1$. The key step passes $\rho\to0$ in the identity on $SM_\rho$ by dominated convergence.

nodes.name: Assume (2.38)-(2.40)

nodes.name: Equation (2.38)
Equation (2.39)

nodes.name: Equation (2.40)
Combine
nodes.statement: Combining (\ref{2.40}), (\ref{2.39}) and (\ref{2.38}) with item (3) of Lemma \ref{L.2.2}, we find \begin{equation} (1-k^+)\int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}+(n-2) \int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert Hu\vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}\leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Combine with Lemma 2.2(3) to get (2.41).

nodes.name: Equation (2.41)
nodes.statement: (1-k^+)\int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}+(n-2) \int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert Hu\vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}\leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}.

nodes.name: Use $k^+<1$
nodes.statement: For $k^+<1$ and $n\geq 2$, we deduce the estimate \begin{equation} \int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Since $k^+<1$, control $\int|\overset{h}{\nabla}u|^2$.

nodes.name: Equation (2.42)
nodes.statement: \int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}.

nodes.name: Bound $Hu$
nodes.statement: In view of the definition of $H$, in (\ref{2.30}), there exists a constant $C$ such that $$ \vert Hu \vert^2 \leq C \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 . $$
nodes.statement_short: $|Hu|\le C|\overset{h}{\nabla}u|$.

nodes.name: Conclude the theorem
nodes.statement: Using the item (2) of Lemma \ref{L.2.2} and (\ref{2.30}), we conclude that $$ \Vert f \Vert ^2_{L^2(S\mathrm{M})}=\int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert Hu \vert^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}\leq C \int_{S\mathrm{M}} \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2 \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \leq C\Vert\mathcal{I} f \Vert^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M})}, $$ and the Theorem \ref{theorem} is done.
nodes.statement_short: $Hu=-f$ yields $\|f\|_{L^2}\le C\|\mathcal{I}f\|_{H^1}$.

nodes.name: Return to the postponed claims
nodes.statement: Now, we come back to prove (\ref{2.38})-(\ref{2.39}) and (\ref{2.40}).

nodes.statement_short: Bound the curvature term using $K^+$ and Lemma 2.3.

Apply Lemma 2.3

Proof of (2.38)
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the Pestov identity over $SM_\rho$ and let $\rho\to0$.

nodes.name: Pestov identity for $u$
nodes.statement_short: Pestov's identity with $Hu=-f$ gives (2.45).

Integrate over $SM_\rho$

nodes.name: Identity on $SM_\rho$
nodes.statement_short: $\langle W,\xi\rangle=|Hu|^2$ gives (2.46).

nodes.name: Equation (2.46)
Set up dominated convergence
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite (2.46) on $SM$ with $\chi_\rho$ and the projection $p$.

nodes.name: Equation (2.47)
What remains for convergence
nodes.statement: Note that all the integrands of (\ref{2.47}) are smooth on $S\mathrm{M} \setminus \partial S \mathrm{M}$ and so, they converge towards their values almost everywhere, when $\rho \rightarrow 0$. Since the functions $\vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2$ and $\vert Hu\vert ^2$ are positive and the second function satifies (\ref{2.43}), then the left side of (\ref{2.47}) converges as $\rho \rightarrow 0$. To apply the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem in (\ref{2.47}), it remains to prove that $\vert \langle V, \nu \rangle p_* \vert$ is bounded by a summable function on $\partial S \mathrm{M}$ which does not depend on $\rho$.
nodes.statement_short: Left side converges; need a $\rho$-independent summable bound on the boundary term.

nodes.name: Tangential derivatives
nodes.statement_short: Introduce tangential horizontal and vertical derivatives on $\partial SM$.

nodes.name: Boundary integrand is bounded
nodes.statement_short: $\langle V,\nu\rangle$ involves only tangential derivatives, which are locally bounded.

nodes.name: Equation (2.48)
Limit $\rho\to0$
nodes.statement_short: Dominated convergence yields (2.38).

nodes.name: Proof of (2.39)
nodes.statement_short: The boundary term is a quadratic first-order form in $\mathcal{I}f$, bounded by its $H^1$ norm.

nodes.name: Boundary term in terms of $\mathcal{I}f$
nodes.statement_short: Use $u=\mathcal{I}f$ on $\partial_+SM$ and $u=0$ on $\partial_-SM$.

nodes.name: Bound by $H^1$ norm
nodes.statement: Consequently, there exists a constant $C$ such that we have $$ \vert \int_{\partial_+ S \mathrm{M}} \mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{I} f) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} \vert \leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert ^2_{H^1(\partial_+ S \mathrm{M})}. $$ This completes the proof of the Theorem \ref{theorem}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound by $C\|\mathcal{I}f\|_{H^1}^2$ and conclude.

nodes.name: First transport equation
nodes.statement: We want to find a function $\theta\in \mathcal{V}(Q)$ which solves the first transport equation \begin{equation} \partial_t \theta+\seq{d\varrho,d\theta}+\frac{1}{2} (\Delta \varrho)\theta=0,\qquad \forall t\in\mathbb{R},\, x\in\mathrm{M}, \end{equation} where $\varrho$ is given by Lemma \ref{L.3.1}.

nodes.name: Equation (3.11)
nodes.statement: \partial_t \theta+\seq{d\varrho,d\theta}+\frac{1}{2} (\Delta \varrho)\theta=0,\qquad \forall t\in\mathbb{R},\, x\in\mathrm{M},

nodes.name: Second transport equation
nodes.statement: Moreover for $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M}) $, we need to find a function $\psi_a\in\mathcal{W}(Q) $ which solves the second transport equation \begin{equation} \partial_t \psi_a+\seq{d\varrho,d\psi_a}+\frac{a}{2}\psi_a=0,\qquad \forall t\in\mathbb{R},\, x\in\mathrm{M}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Equation (3.12)
nodes.statement: \partial_t \psi_a+\seq{d\varrho,d\psi_a}+\frac{a}{2}\psi_a=0,\qquad \forall t\in\mathbb{R},\, x\in\mathrm{M}.

nodes.name: Solution of the first transport equation
nodes.statement: The first step is to solve the transport equation (\ref{3.11}). Recall that if $f(r)$ is any function of the geodesic distance $r$, then \begin{equation} \Delta_{\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}}f(r)=f''(r)+\frac{\alpha^{-1}}{2}\frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial r}f'(r). \end{equation} Here $\alpha=\alpha(r,\xi)$ denotes the square of the volume element in geodesic polar coordinates. The transport equation (\ref{3.11}) becomes \begin{equation} \frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial \widetilde{\varrho}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{4}\widetilde{\theta}\alpha^{-1}\frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial r}\frac{\partial \widetilde{\varrho}}{\partial r}=0. \end{equation} Thus $\widetilde{\theta}$ satisfies \begin{equation} \frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{4}\widetilde{\theta}\alpha^{-1}\frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial r}=0. \end{equation} Let $\phi\in\mathcal{C}_0^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ and $\Psi\in H^2(S^+_y\mathrm{M})$. Let us write $\widetilde{\theta}$ in the form \begin{equation} \widetilde{\theta}(t,r,\xi)=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi). \end{equation} Direct computations yield \begin{equation} \frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial t}(t,r,\xi)=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi'(t-r)\Psi(\xi), \end{equation} and, we find \begin{equation} \frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial r}(t,r,\xi)=-\frac{1}{4}\alpha^{-5/4}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial r}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi)-\alpha^{-1/4}\phi'(t-r)\Psi(\xi). \end{equation} Finally, (\ref{3.18}) and (\ref{3.17}) yield \begin{equation} \frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial t}(t,r,\xi)+\frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial r}(t,r,\xi)=-\frac{1}{4}\alpha^{-1}\widetilde{\theta}(t,r,\xi)\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial r}. \end{equation} Now if we assume that $\mathrm{supp}(\phi) \subset (0,\epsilon)$, then for any $x=\exp_y(r\xi)\in \mathrm{M}$, it is easy to see that $$ \partial_t^j\widetilde{\theta}(0,r,\xi)=\partial_t^j\widetilde{\theta}(T,r,\xi)=0,\quad j=0,1,2,\,\, T-r>\varepsilon. $$
nodes.statement_short: In polar coordinates the ansatz $\widetilde\theta=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi)$ solves (3.11), vanishing at $t=0,T$.

nodes.name: Equation (3.13)
nodes.statement: \Delta_{\widetilde{\mathrm{g}}}f(r)=f''(r)+\frac{\alpha^{-1}}{2}\frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial r}f'(r).

nodes.name: Square of the volume element in polar coordinates
nodes.statement: Here $\alpha=\alpha(r,\xi)$ denotes the square of the volume element in geodesic polar coordinates.

nodes.name: Equation (3.14)
nodes.statement: \frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial \widetilde{\varrho}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{4}\widetilde{\theta}\alpha^{-1}\frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial r}\frac{\partial \widetilde{\varrho}}{\partial r}=0.

nodes.name: Equation (3.15)
nodes.statement: \frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{4}\widetilde{\theta}\alpha^{-1}\frac{\partial \alpha}{\partial r}=0.

nodes.name: Equation (3.16)
nodes.statement: \widetilde{\theta}(t,r,\xi)=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi).

nodes.name: Equation (3.17)
nodes.statement: \frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial t}(t,r,\xi)=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi'(t-r)\Psi(\xi),

nodes.name: Equation (3.18)
nodes.statement: \frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial r}(t,r,\xi)=-\frac{1}{4}\alpha^{-5/4}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial r}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi)-\alpha^{-1/4}\phi'(t-r)\Psi(\xi).

nodes.name: Equation (3.19)
nodes.statement: \frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial t}(t,r,\xi)+\frac{\partial \widetilde{\theta}}{\partial r}(t,r,\xi)=-\frac{1}{4}\alpha^{-1}\widetilde{\theta}(t,r,\xi)\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial r}.

nodes.name: Solution of the second transport equation
nodes.statement: For the second transport equation (\ref{3.12}), in polar coordinates, takes the form \begin{equation} \frac{\partial \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial \widetilde{\varrho}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\partial r} +\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)\widetilde{\psi}_a=0, \end{equation} where $\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi):=a(\theta_r(y,\xi))$. Thus $\widetilde{\psi}_a$ satisfies \begin{equation} \frac{\partial \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)\widetilde{\psi}_a=0. \end{equation} Thus, we can choose $\widetilde{\psi}_a$ as following \begin{equation} \widetilde{\psi}_a(t,y,r,\xi)=\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^t\widetilde{a}(r-s,y,\xi)ds}. \end{equation} Since $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M})$, we get $\psi_a\in \mathcal{W}(Q)$. Hence (\ref{3.12}) is solved.
nodes.statement_short: Integrating along $t-r=$const gives $\widetilde\psi_a=\exp(-\frac12\int_0^t\widetilde a(r-s)ds)$ solving (3.12).

nodes.name: Equation (3.20)
nodes.statement: \frac{\partial \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial \widetilde{\varrho}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\partial r} +\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)\widetilde{\psi}_a=0,

nodes.name: Equation (3.21)
nodes.statement: \frac{\partial \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial \widetilde{\psi}_a}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)\widetilde{\psi}_a=0.

nodes.name: Equation (3.22)
nodes.statement: \widetilde{\psi}_a(t,y,r,\xi)=\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^t\widetilde{a}(r-s,y,\xi)ds}.

nodes.name: Phase function $\varphi$
nodes.statement: We introduce the function \begin{equation} \varphi(x,t):=\varrho(x)-t,\quad x\in\mathrm{M},\,\, t\in (0,T), \end{equation} where $\varrho$ is given by Lemma \ref{L.3.1}.

nodes.name: Equation (3.23)
nodes.statement: \varphi(x,t):=\varrho(x)-t,\quad x\in\mathrm{M},\,\, t\in (0,T),

nodes.name: Geometric optics solutions of the damped wave equation
nodes.statement: Let $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M})$, $q\in W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M})$, and $\theta\in\mathcal{V}(Q)$, $\psi_{a}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ solve respectively (\ref{3.11}) and (\ref{3.12}). Then for all $h>0$ small enough, there exists a solution $$ u(x,t;h)\in \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap\mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\mathrm{M}))\cap\mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})) $$ of the wave equation \begin{equation*} (\partial^2_t-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x))u=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad Q, \end{equation*} with the initial condition \begin{equation*} u(x,0)=\partial_tu(x,0)=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad \mathrm{M}, \end{equation*} of the form \begin{equation} u(x,t)=\theta(x,t)\psi_a(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_h(x,t), \end{equation} the remainder $r_h(x,t)$ is such that \begin{align*} r_h(x,t)&=0,\quad (x,t)\in \Sigma , \\ r_h(x,0)=\partial_t r_h(x,0)&=0,\quad x\in \mathrm{M}. \end{align*} Furthermore, there exist $C>0$, $h_0>0$ such that, for all $h \leq h_0$ the following estimates hold true. \begin{equation} \sum_{k=0}^2 \sum_{j=0}^{k} h^{k-1} \|\partial_t^{j} r_h(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{k-j}(\mathrm{M})}\leq C\norm{\theta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}. \end{equation} The constant $C$ depends only on $T$ and $\mathrm{M}$ (that is $C$ does not depend on $a$ and $h$).
nodes.statement_short: WKB solutions $u=\theta\psi_a e^{i\varphi/h}+r_h$ with remainder bounded uniformly in $a,h$.
assumptions: Let $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M})$, $q\in W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M})$, and $\theta\in\mathcal{V}(Q)$, $\psi_{a}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ solve respectively (\ref{3.11}) and (\ref{3.12}).
conclusions: Furthermore, there exist $C>0$, $h_0>0$ such that, for all $h \leq h_0$ the following estimates hold true.
nodes.label: L.3.2

nodes.name: Equation (3.24)
nodes.statement: u(x,t)=\theta(x,t)\psi_a(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_h(x,t),

nodes.name: Equation (3.25)
nodes.statement: \sum_{k=0}^2 \sum_{j=0}^{k} h^{k-1} \|\partial_t^{j} r_h(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{k-j}(\mathrm{M})}\leq C\norm{\theta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement_short: Write the remainder as the solution of the damped wave equation with source $V_h$; eikonal and transport equations kill the singular terms. Energy estimates (Lemma 1.1), applied also to the time-primitive $r_h^*$, give the $h$-weighted bounds.

nodes.name: Remainder problem
nodes.statement: Let $r(x,t;h)$ solves the following homogenous boundary value problem \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{array}{llll} \para{\partial^2_t-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x)}r(x,t)=V_h (x,t) & \textrm{in }\,\, Q,\cr r(x,0)=\partial_tr(x,0)=0,& \textrm{in }\,\,\mathrm{M},\cr r(x,t)=0 & \textrm{on} \,\, \Sigma. \end{array} \right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define the remainder as solution of the damped wave equation with source $V_h$.

nodes.name: Equation (3.26)
nodes.statement: \left\{ \begin{array}{llll} \para{\partial^2_t-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x)}r(x,t)=V_h (x,t) & \textrm{in }\,\, Q,\cr r(x,0)=\partial_tr(x,0)=0,& \textrm{in }\,\,\mathrm{M},\cr r(x,t)=0 & \textrm{on} \,\, \Sigma. \end{array} \right.

nodes.name: Equation (3.27)
nodes.statement: V_h(x,t)=-\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x)}\para{(\theta\psi_a)(x,t)e^{i\varphi/h}}.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: To prove our Lemma it would be enough to show that $r$ satisfies the estimates (\ref{3.25}).
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to bound the remainder.

nodes.name: Expand the source term
nodes.statement: By a simple computation, we have \begin{align} -V_h (x,t)&=e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x)}\para{(\theta\psi_a)( x,t)}\cr &\quad -\frac{2i}{h} e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\psi_a(x,t)\para{\partial_t\theta+\seq{d\varrho,d\theta}+\frac{\theta}{2}\Delta\varrho}( x,t)\cr &\quad -\frac{2i}{h} e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\theta(x,t)\para{\partial_t\psi_a+\seq{d\varrho,d\psi_a}+\frac{a}{2} \psi_a}(x,t)\cr &\quad-\frac{1}{h^2} \theta\psi_a(x,t) e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\para{1-\abs{d\varrho}^2}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Expand $V_h$ in powers of $h^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Equation (3.28)
nodes.statement: -V_h (x,t)&=e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x)}\para{(\theta\psi_a)( x,t)}\cr &\quad -\frac{2i}{h} e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\psi_a(x,t)\para{\partial_t\theta+\seq{d\varrho,d\theta}+\frac{\theta}{2}\Delta\varrho}( x,t)\cr &\quad -\frac{2i}{h} e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\theta(x,t)\para{\partial_t\psi_a+\seq{d\varrho,d\psi_a}+\frac{a}{2} \psi_a}(x,t)\cr &\quad-\frac{1}{h^2} \theta\psi_a(x,t) e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\para{1-\abs{d\varrho}^2}.

nodes.name: Eikonal and transport cancellation
nodes.statement: Taking into account (\ref{3.7})-(\ref{3.11}) and (\ref{3.12}), the right-hand side of (\ref{3.28}) becomes \begin{align} V_h (x,t)&=-e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}(\partial_t^2-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x))\para{(\theta\psi_a)(x,t)} \cr &\equiv-e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}V_0(x,t). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Eikonal and transport equations kill the $h^{-1}$ and $h^{-2}$ terms.

nodes.name: Equation (3.29)
nodes.statement: V_h (x,t)&=-e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}(\partial_t^2-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x))\para{(\theta\psi_a)(x,t)} \cr &\equiv-e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}V_0(x,t).

nodes.name: Bound on $V_0$
nodes.statement_short: Bound $V_0$ and $\partial_tV_0$ by $\|\theta\|_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}$.

nodes.name: Equation (3.30)
nodes.statement:
orm{V_0}_{L^2(Q)}+
orm{\partial_tV_0}_{L^2(Q)}\leq C
orm{	heta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.

nodes.name: Regularity of the remainder
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{L.1.1}, we find \begin{equation} r_h\in \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap\mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1_0(\mathrm{M}))\cap\mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 1.1 gives regularity of $r_h$.

nodes.name: Equation (3.31)
nodes.statement: r_h\in \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap\mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1_0(\mathrm{M}))\cap\mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})).

nodes.name: Time primitive
nodes.statement: Since the coefficients $a$ and $q$ do not depend on $t$, the function $$ r^*_h(x,t)=\int_0^tr_h(x,s)ds, $$ solves the mixed hyperbolic problem (\ref{3.26}) with the right side $$ V^*_h(x,t)=\int_0^tV_h (x,s)ds=-ih\int_0^tV_0(x,s)\partial_s\para{e^{i\varphi(x,s)/h}}ds. $$
nodes.statement_short: The time-primitive $r_h^*$ solves the problem with source $V_h^*$.

nodes.name: $L^2$ bound of order $h$
nodes.statement_short: Integration by parts and (1.5) give $\|r_h\|_{L^2}\le Ch\|\theta\|$.

nodes.statement:
orm{r_h(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}=
orm{\partial_tr^*_h(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq Ch

Conclude
nodes.statement: Collecting (\ref{3.32})-(\ref{3.33}) and (\ref{3.34}) we get (\ref{3.25}). The proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Collect the bounds into (3.25).

nodes.name: Geometric optics solutions of the backward damped wave equation
nodes.statement: Let $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M})$, $q\in W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M})$, and $\theta\in\mathcal{V}(Q)$, $\psi_{-a}\mathcal{W}(Q)$ solve respectively (\ref{3.11}) and (\ref{3.12}) (with $a$ replaced by $-a$). Then for all $h>0$ small enough, there exists a solution $$ u(x,t;h)\in \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap\mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\mathrm{M}))\cap\mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})) $$ of the wave equation \begin{equation*} (\partial^2_t-\Delta-a(x)\partial_t+q(x))u=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad Q, \end{equation*} with the final condition \begin{equation*} u(T,x)=\partial_tu(T,x)=0,\quad \textrm{in}\quad \mathrm{M}, \end{equation*} of the form \begin{equation} u(x,t;h)=\theta(x,t)\psi_{-a}(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_h(x,t), \end{equation} the remainder $r_h(t,x)$ is such that \begin{align*} r_h(x,t)&=0,\quad (x,t)\in \Sigma , \\ r_h(x,T)=\partial_tr_h(x,T)&=0,\quad x\in \mathrm{M}. \end{align*} Furthermore, there exist $C>0$, $h_0>0$ such that, for all $h \leq h_0$ the following estimates hold true. \begin{equation} \sum_{k=0}^2 \sum_{j=0}^{k} h^{k-1} \|\partial_t^{j} r_h(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{k-j}(\mathrm{M})}\leq C\norm{\theta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}. \end{equation} The constant $C$ depends only on $T$ and $\mathrm{M}$ (that is $C$ does not depend on $a$ and $h$).
nodes.statement_short: Analogue of Lemma 3.2 for $-a$ with final conditions at $t=T$.
assumptions: Let $a\in W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M})$, $q\in W^{2,\infty}(\mathrm{M})$, and $\theta\in\mathcal{V}(Q)$, $\psi_{-a}\mathcal{W}(Q)$ solve respectively (\ref{3.11}) and (\ref{3.12}) (with $a$ replaced by $-a$).
conclusions: Furthermore, there exist $C>0$, $h_0>0$ such that, for all $h \leq h_0$ the following estimates hold true.
nodes.label: L.3.3

nodes.name: Equation (3.35)
nodes.statement: u(x,t;h)=\theta(x,t)\psi_{-a}(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_h(x,t),

nodes.name: Equation (3.36)
nodes.statement: \sum_{k=0}^2 \sum_{j=0}^{k} h^{k-1} \|\partial_t^{j} r_h(\cdot,t)\|_{H^{k-j}(\mathrm{M})}\leq C\norm{\theta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.

nodes.name: Coefficient differences $a$ and $q$
nodes.statement: As before, we let $a_1,\,a_2\in\mathscr{A}(m_1,\eta)$ and $q_1,q_2\in\mathscr{Q}(m_2)$ such that $a_1=a_2$, $q_1=q_2$ near the boundary $\partial\mathrm{M}$. We set $$ a(x)=(a_1-a_2)(x),\quad q(x)=(q_1-q_2)(x). $$

nodes.name: Product amplitude $\psi_a$
nodes.statement: We denote $\psi_{a_2}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ and $\psi_{-a_1}\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ the solutions of (\ref{3.12}) respectively with $a=a_2$ and $a=-a_1$ given by (\ref{3.22}), and set \begin{equation} \psi_a(x,t)=\psi_{a_2}(x,t)\psi_{-a_1}(x,t). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Equation (4.1)
nodes.statement: \psi_a(x,t)=\psi_{a_2}(x,t)\psi_{-a_1}(x,t).

nodes.name: Preliminary estimate for the absorption coefficient
nodes.statement_short: The weighted integral of $a\,\theta_2\bar\theta_1\psi_a$ is bounded by $C(h+h^{-2}\|\Lambda_1-\Lambda_2\|)$.
assumptions: for any $\theta_j\in \mathcal{V}(Q)$, $j=1,2$, satisfying the transport equation (\ref{3.7})
nodes.label: L.4.1

nodes.name: Equation (4.2)
Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement_short: Plug a forward GO solution for $(a_2,q_2)$ and a backward GO solution for $(-a_1,q_1)$ into Green's formula. The leading $h^{-1}$ term isolates $a$; the DN-map difference is bounded via the trace theorem.

orm{r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+

nodes.name: Solution with coefficients $(a_1,q_1)$
nodes.statement: Let us denote by $f_h$ the function $$ f_h(x,t)=(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h},\quad (x,t)\in\Sigma, $$ and we consider $v$ the solution of the following non-homogenous boundary value problem \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{array}{lll} \para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)} v=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, Q,\cr v(x,0)=\partial_tv(x,0)=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, \mathrm{M},\cr v(x,t)=u_2(x,t):=f_{h}(x,t), & \textrm{on}\,\, \Sigma. \end{array} \right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Solve the $(a_1,q_1)$ problem with Dirichlet data $f_h$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.5)
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{lll} \para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)} v=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, Q,\cr v(x,0)=\partial_tv(x,0)=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, \mathrm{M},\cr v(x,t)=u_2(x,t):=f_{h}(x,t), & \textrm{on}\,\, \Sigma. \end{array} \right.

nodes.name: Difference $w$
nodes.statement: We let $ w=v-u_2$. Therefore, $w$ solves the following homogenous boundary value problem $$ \left\{\begin{array}{lll} \para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}w(x,t)=a(x)\partial_tu_2(x,t)+q(x)u_2(x,t) & \textrm{in}\,\, Q,\cr w(x,0)=\partial_tw(x,0)=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, \mathrm{M},\cr w(x,t)=0, & \textrm{on}\,\, \Sigma. \end{array} \right. $$
nodes.statement_short: The difference $w=v-u_2$ solves an equation with source $a\partial_tu_2+qu_2$.

nodes.name: Regularity of $w$
nodes.statement: Using the fact that $a(x)\partial_tu_2+q(x)u_2 \in W^{1,1}(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))$ with $u_2(\cdot,0)=\partial_t u_2(\cdot,0)\equiv 0$, by Lemma \ref{L.1.1}, we deduce that $$ w\in \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})\cap H^1_0(\mathrm{M})). $$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 1.1 gives regularity of $w$.

nodes.name: Backward GO solution
nodes.statement: Therefore, we have constructed a special solution $$ \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\mathrm{M})) \cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})), $$ to the backward wave equation \begin{align*} \para{\partial_t^2-\Delta-a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}u_1(x,t)&=0, \quad (x,t) \in Q, \\ u_1(x,T)=u_1(x,T)&=0, \quad x \in \mathrm{M}, \end{align*} having the special form \begin{equation} u_1(x,t)=(\theta_1\psi_{-a_1})( t,x)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_{1,h}(x,t), \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Construct a backward GO solution $u_1$ for $(-a_1,q_1)$ with remainder bound (4.7).

nodes.name: Equation (4.6)
nodes.statement: u_1(x,t)=(\theta_1\psi_{-a_1})( t,x)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_{1,h}(x,t),

nodes.name: Equation (4.7)
Green's formula
nodes.statement: Integrating by parts and using Green's formula (\ref{3.4}), we find \begin{multline} \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M}\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}w\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t = \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tu_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t\cr +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t =-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \partial_\nu w\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t. \end{multline}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate by parts against $\bar u_1$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.8)
nodes.statement: \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M}\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}w\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t = \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tu_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t\cr +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t =-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \partial_\nu w\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t.

nodes.name: Boundary term as DN-map difference
nodes.statement: Taking (\ref{4.8}), (\ref{4.6}) into account, we deduce \begin{multline} -\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tu_2\overline{u}_1(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t =\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}}\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2,q_2}} f_{h}(x,t)\overline{g}_h(x,t) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t\cr +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t \end{multline} where $g_h$ is given by $$ g_h(x,t)=(\theta_1\psi_{-a_1})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h},\quad (x,t)\in \Sigma. $$
nodes.statement_short: Express the boundary term via $\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.9)
nodes.statement: -\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tu_2\overline{u}_1(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t =\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}}\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2,q_2}} f_{h}(x,t)\overline{g}_h(x,t) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t\cr +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t

nodes.name: Isolate the leading term
nodes.statement: It follows from (\ref{4.9}), (\ref{4.6}) and (\ref{4.3}) that \begin{multline} ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\theta_2 \overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)(\psi_{a_2}\psi_{-a_1})( x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t =\cr \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t -ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(t,x)e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t r_{2,h}(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1})(x,t) e^{-i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tr_{2,h}(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2(x,t)\overline{u}_1(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt \cr = \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h \para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t+\mathscr{R}_h. \end{multline}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the GO forms to isolate $ih^{-1}\int a\theta_2\bar\theta_1\psi_a$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.10)
nodes.statement: ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\theta_2 \overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)(\psi_{a_2}\psi_{-a_1})( x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t =\cr \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t -ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(t,x)e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_t r_{2,h}(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1})(x,t) e^{-i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x)\partial_tr_{2,h}(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr +\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x)u_2(x,t)\overline{u}_1(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt \cr = \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h \para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t+\mathscr{R}_h.

nodes.name: Remainder bound
nodes.statement: In view of (\ref{4.7}) and (\ref{4.4}), we have \begin{equation} \abs{\mathscr{R}_h}\leq C\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\mathscr{R}_h$ by the remainder estimates.

nodes.name: Equation (4.11)
nodes.statement: \abs{\mathscr{R}_h}\leq C\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.

nodes.name: Boundary term bound
nodes.statement_short: Trace theorem bounds the DN term by $Ch^{-3}$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.12)
Conclude
nodes.statement: The estimate (\ref{4.2}) follows easily from (\ref{4.10}), (\ref{4.11}) and (\ref{4.12}).\\ This completes the proof of the Lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Combine to obtain (4.2).

nodes.name: Estimate on the X-ray transform of the absorption coefficient
nodes.statement: There exists $C>0$ such that for any $\Psi\in H^2 (S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})$, the following estimate \begin{multline} \abs{\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\para{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)}-1} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)}\cr \leq C\para{h+h^{-2}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}} \norm{\Psi}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})}. \end{multline} holds for any $y\in\partial\mathrm{M}_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Tested against $\Psi$, $\exp(-\frac12\mathcal{I}a)-1$ is bounded by $C(h+h^{-2}\|\Lambda_1-\Lambda_2\|)\|\Psi\|_{H^2}$.
nodes.label: L.4.2

nodes.name: Equation (4.13)
nodes.statement: \abs{\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\para{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)}-1} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)}\cr \leq C\para{h+h^{-2}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}} \norm{\Psi}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: We take two solutions to (\ref{3.11}) of the form \begin{align*} \widetilde{\theta}_1(t,r,\xi)&=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi), \\ \widetilde{\theta}_2(t,r,\xi)&=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r). \end{align*} Now we change variable in the left term of (\ref{4.1}), $x=\exp_{y}(r\xi)$, $r>0$ and $\xi\in S_{y}\mathrm{M}_1$, we have \begin{multline} \int_0^T\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\overline{\theta}_1\theta_2)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t) \,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t \cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)(\overline{\widetilde{\theta}}_1\widetilde{\theta}_2)( t,r,\xi) \widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t,r,\xi) \alpha^{1/2} \, \mathrm{d} r \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)\phi^2( t-r)\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t,r,\xi)\Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} r \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_\mathbb{R} \widetilde{a}( t-\tau,y,\xi)\phi^2(\tau)\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t, t-\tau,\xi)\Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_\mathbb{R} \widetilde{a}( t-\tau,y,\xi)\phi^2(\tau)\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ t}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)\cr =2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\int_0^T \frac{d}{dt}\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ t}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)\cr =2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ T}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}-1} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi). \end{multline} By the support properties of the function $\phi$, we get that the left-hand side term in (\ref{4.14}) reads \begin{multline*} \int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{T}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}-1} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)=\cr \int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(s,y,\xi)ds}-1} \Psi(\xi) \mu(y,\xi) \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi). \end{multline*} Then, by (\ref{4.14}) and (\ref{4.2}) we get \begin{multline} \abs{\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\para{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)}-1} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)}\cr \leq C\para{h+h^{-2}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}} \norm{\Psi}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})}. \end{multline} This completes the proof of the Lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\theta_j$ of the form $\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi$ in Lemma 4.1 and change to polar coordinates; the $t$-integral telescopes to $\exp(-\frac12\mathcal{I}a)-1$.

nodes.name: Special amplitudes
nodes.statement: We take two solutions to (\ref{3.11}) of the form \begin{align*} \widetilde{\theta}_1(t,r,\xi)&=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi(\xi), \\ \widetilde{\theta}_2(t,r,\xi)&=\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\theta_1,\theta_2$ of the form $\alpha^{-1/4}\phi(t-r)\Psi$.

nodes.name: Polar change of variables
nodes.statement: Now we change variable in the left term of (\ref{4.1}), $x=\exp_{y}(r\xi)$, $r>0$ and $\xi\in S_{y}\mathrm{M}_1$, we have \begin{multline} \int_0^T\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\overline{\theta}_1\theta_2)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t) \,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t \cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)(\overline{\widetilde{\theta}}_1\widetilde{\theta}_2)( t,r,\xi) \widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t,r,\xi) \alpha^{1/2} \, \mathrm{d} r \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)\phi^2( t-r)\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t,r,\xi)\Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} r \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_\mathbb{R} \widetilde{a}( t-\tau,y,\xi)\phi^2(\tau)\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t, t-\tau,\xi)\Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_\mathbb{R} \widetilde{a}( t-\tau,y,\xi)\phi^2(\tau)\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ t}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)\cr =2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\int_0^T \frac{d}{dt}\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ t}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)\cr =2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ T}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}-1} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi). \end{multline}
nodes.statement_short: Change to polar coordinates; the integrand becomes a time derivative of the exponential.

nodes.name: Equation (4.14)
nodes.statement: \int_0^T\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} a(x) (\overline{\theta}_1\theta_2)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t) \,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t \cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)(\overline{\widetilde{\theta}}_1\widetilde{\theta}_2)( t,r,\xi) \widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t,r,\xi) \alpha^{1/2} \, \mathrm{d} r \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(r,y,\xi)\phi^2( t-r)\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t,r,\xi)\Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} r \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_\mathbb{R} \widetilde{a}( t-\tau,y,\xi)\phi^2(\tau)\widetilde{\psi}_{a}( t, t-\tau,\xi)\Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_\mathbb{R} \widetilde{a}( t-\tau,y,\xi)\phi^2(\tau)\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ t}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)\cr =2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\int_0^T \frac{d}{dt}\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ t}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)\cr =2\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{ T}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}-1} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi).

nodes.name: Support of $\phi$
nodes.statement: By the support properties of the function $\phi$, we get that the left-hand side term in (\ref{4.14}) reads \begin{multline*} \int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(\tau) \!\!\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{T}\widetilde{a}(s-\tau,y,\xi)ds}-1} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)=\cr \int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\cro{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{a}(s,y,\xi)ds}-1} \Psi(\xi) \mu(y,\xi) \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi). \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Support of $\phi$ turns the integral into the X-ray transform.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Then, by (\ref{4.14}) and (\ref{4.2}) we get \begin{multline} \abs{\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\para{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)}-1} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)}\cr \leq C\para{h+h^{-2}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}} \norm{\Psi}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})}. \end{multline} This completes the proof of the Lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Combine with Lemma 4.1 estimate (4.2).

nodes.name: Equation (4.15)
nodes.statement: \abs{\int_{S^+_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\para{\exp\para{-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)}-1} \Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)}\cr \leq C\para{h+h^{-2}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}} \norm{\Psi}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_{1})}.

nodes.name: Poisson kernel of the unit ball in $T_y\mathrm{M}_1$
nodes.statement: We define the Poisson kernel of $B(0,1)\subset T_y \mathrm{M}_1$, i.e., $$ P(\theta,\xi)=\frac{1-\abs{\theta}^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\theta-\xi}^n},\quad \theta\in B(0,1);\,\, \xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}_1. $$
nodes.section: 4.2 End of the proof of the stability estimate of the absorption coefficient

nodes.name: Scaled Poisson kernel $\Psi_\kappa$
nodes.statement: For $0<\kappa<1$, we define $\Psi_\kappa: S_y\mathrm{M}_1\times S_y\mathrm{M}_1\to \mathbb{R}$ as \begin{align} \Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi)=P(\kappa\theta,\xi). \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.2 End of the proof of the stability estimate of the absorption coefficient

nodes.name: Equation (4.16)
nodes.statement: \Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi)=P(\kappa\theta,\xi).
nodes.section: 4.2 End of the proof of the stability estimate of the absorption coefficient

nodes.name: Properties of the scaled Poisson kernel
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi_\kappa$ given by (\ref{4.16}), $\kappa \in (0,1)$. Then we have the following properties: \begin{equation} \displaystyle 0\leq\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi)\leq \frac{2}{\alpha_n(1-\kappa)^{n-1}},\quad \forall\, \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\xi,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1. \end{equation} \begin{equation} \displaystyle \int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) d\omega_y(\xi)=1,\quad \forall \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1. \end{equation} \begin{equation} \int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) \abs{\theta-\xi}d\omega_y(\xi)\leq C(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}, \quad \forall\, \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1. \end{equation} \begin{equation} \norm{ \Psi_\kappa(\theta,\cdot)}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_1)}^2\leq \frac{C}{(1-\kappa)^{n+3}}, \quad \forall \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4.2 End of the proof of the stability estimate of the absorption coefficient
nodes.statement_short: $\Psi_\kappa$ is a bounded, normalised approximate identity with $H^2$ norm $O((1-\kappa)^{-(n+3)/2})$.
conclusions: Then we have the following properties:
nodes.label: L.4.3

nodes.name: Equation (4.17)
nodes.statement: \displaystyle 0\leq\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi)\leq \frac{2}{\alpha_n(1-\kappa)^{n-1}},\quad \forall\, \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\xi,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
nodes.section: 4.2 End of the proof of the stability estimate of the absorption coefficient

nodes.name: Equation (4.18)
nodes.statement: \displaystyle \int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) d\omega_y(\xi)=1,\quad \forall \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
nodes.section: 4.2 End of the proof of the stability estimate of the absorption coefficient

nodes.name: Equation (4.19)
nodes.statement: \int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) \abs{\theta-\xi}d\omega_y(\xi)\leq C(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}, \quad \forall\, \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
nodes.section: 4.2 End of the proof of the stability estimate of the absorption coefficient

nodes.name: Equation (4.20)
nodes.statement: \norm{ \Psi_\kappa(\theta,\cdot)}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_1)}^2\leq \frac{C}{(1-\kappa)^{n+3}}, \quad \forall \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
nodes.section: 4.2 End of the proof of the stability estimate of the absorption coefficient

nodes.name: Pointwise estimate of the X-ray transform of the absorption coefficient
nodes.statement: Let $a_{i}\in \mathscr{A}(m_{1},\alpha)$, $q_i \in \mathscr{Q}(m_2)$, $i=1,\,2$. There exist $C>0,$ $\delta>0$, $\beta>0$ and $h_{0}>0$ such that \begin{equation} |\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)|\leq C \Big( h^{-\delta}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h^{\beta} \Big),\quad\forall \, (y,\theta)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1, \end{equation} for any $h\leq h_{0}$. Here $C$ depends only on $\mathrm{M}$, $T$, $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$.
nodes.section: 4.2 End of the proof of the stability estimate of the absorption coefficient

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement: Let $(y,\theta)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1$ be a fixed and let $\Psi_\kappa$ be the positive function given by (\ref{4.16}). We extend $\mathcal{I}(a)$ by zero in $\partial_-S\mathrm{M}$, then, we have \begin{multline} \Big|\exp\para{-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)} -1 \Big|=\Big| \displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\Big[ \exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big)-1 \Big]\,d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|\cr \leq\quad \Big| \displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\Big[\exp\Big( -\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big) -\exp\Big(-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)\Big) \Big] \,d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|\cr +\Big| \displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1} \Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\Big[\exp\Big(-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi) \Big)-1 \Big] d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|. \end{multline} Therefore, since we have $$\begin{array}{lll} \Big| \!\exp\Big( \!-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)\Big) \!-\!\exp\Big(\! -\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi) \! \Big) \Big|\!\!\!&\leq&\!\!\! C\Big|\displaystyle \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)-\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)\Big|,\cr \end{array}$$ and using the fact that $$ \Big|\displaystyle \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)-\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)\Big|\leq C \,|\theta-\xi|, $$ we deduce upon applying Lemma \ref{L.4.2} with $\Psi=\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\cdot)$ the following estimation \begin{multline*} \Big|\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)\Big)-1 \Big|\leq \cr C\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\,|\theta-\xi|\,d\omega_y(\xi)+C\Big( h^{-2}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h \Big)\|\Psi_{\kappa}\|_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_1)}^{2}. \end{multline*} On the other hand, by (\ref{4.20}) and (\ref{4.19}), we have the following inequality $$ \Big|\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)\Big)-1 \Big|\leq C \,(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}+C\Big( h^{-2}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h \Big)(1-\kappa)^{-(3+n)}. $$ Selecting $(1-\kappa)$ small such that $(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}=h(1-\kappa)^{-(n+3)}$, that is $(1-\kappa)=h^{2n/1+2n^2+6n}$, we find two constants $\delta>0$ and $\beta>0$ such that $$\Big| \exp \Big( -\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big)-1 \Big|\leq C \Big[ h^{-\delta}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h^{\beta} \Big].$$ Now, using the fact that $|X|\leq e^{M}\,|e^{X}-1|$ for any $|X|\leq M$, we deduce that $$\Big| -\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big|\leq e^{M_{1}T}\Big| \exp\Big( -\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big)-1 \Big|.$$ Hence, we conclude that for all $\theta\in S_y\mathrm{M}_1$ and $y\in $ we have $$ \Big|\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big|\leq C \Big(h^{-\delta}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h^{\beta}\Big). $$ The proof of Lemma \ref{L.4.4} is complete.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.4: stability of the absorption coefficient
nodes.statement: Integrating the estimate (\ref{4.21}) over $\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1,$ with respect to $ \mu(y,\theta) \, \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} (y,\theta)$, then minimizing on $h$, we get \begin{equation} \|\mathcal{I}(a)\|_{L^2(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1)}\leq C \|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|^{\frac{\beta}{\beta+\delta}}. \end{equation} With respect to the Theorem \ref{theorem}, we have \begin{equation} \|a\|_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C \|\mathcal{I}(a)\|_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1)}. \end{equation} By interpolation inequality and (\ref{2.7}), we have \begin{align} \|\mathcal{I}(a)\|^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1)} & \leq C \|\mathcal{I}(a)\|_{L^2(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1)}\|\mathcal{I}(a)\|_{H^2(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1)} \cr & \leq C \|\mathcal{I}(a)\|_{L^2(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1)}. \end{align} Combining with (\ref{4.24}) and (\ref{4.25}), we get $$ \|a\|_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C \|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|^{s_0}, $$ where $s_0=\frac{\beta}{2(\beta+\delta)}$.\\ Moreover, let $\eta_0\in (n/2,\eta)$, by Sobolev emedding and interpolation inequality, there exists $\delta\in(0,1)$ such that \begin{align} \|a\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})}\leq\norm{a}_{H^{\eta_0}(\mathrm{M})}\leq C \|a\|^{\delta}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\|a\|^{1-\delta}_{H^\eta(\mathrm{M})}\leq C \|a\|^\delta_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C \|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|^{\delta s_0}. \end{align} This completes the proof of the H\"older stability estimate of the absorption coefficient.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2

We have \begin{multline} \int_0^T\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x) (\overline{\theta}_1\theta_2)(x,t) \,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t \cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{q}(r,y,\xi)(\overline{\widetilde{\theta}}_1\widetilde{\theta}_2)( t,r,\xi) \alpha^{1/2} \, \mathrm{d} r \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t\cr =\int_0^T\!\!\int_{S_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\!\int_0^{\ell_+(y,\xi)}\widetilde{q}(r,y,\xi)\phi^2( t-r)\Psi(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} r \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi) \, \mathrm{d} t. \end{multline} By support properties of the function $\phi$, we get $$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\mathrm{M} q(x) (\overline{\theta}_1\theta_2)(x,t) \,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t=\bigg(\int_\mathbb{R}\phi^2(t)\,dt \bigg) \!\!\int_{S_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\mathcal{I} q(y,\xi) \Psi(\xi) \, \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi). $$ Then, by (\ref{5.2}), we get \begin{equation} \bigg|\int_{S_{y}\mathrm{M}_1}\mathcal{I} q(y,\xi) \Psi(\xi) \, \, \mathrm{d}\omega_y(\xi)\bigg| \leq C\para{h+h^{-1} \|a\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})}+h^{-3}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1} -\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}} } \norm{\Psi}_{H^2(S^+_y\mathrm{M}_{1})}. \end{equation} This compete the proof.
